reference: Masters R, Anwar E, Collins B, Cookson R, Capewell S (2017). Return on investment of public health interventions: a systematic review. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health 71(8):827-834
task: Quantifies the economic return of public health interventions, to make the case for spending on prevention
metrics: Return on investment (how many dollars come back per dollar spent); cost-benefit ratio
geoLevel: National and local, depending on the intervention
inputData: 52 studies included from 2,957 titles screened across seven research databases
output: Pooled return-on-investment estimates: median 14.3 to 1 overall; 4.1 to 1 for local interventions; 27.2 to 1 for national ones
dataSources: Published intervention cost and outcome data from the included studies
accessNote: Not a dataset - a review of published studies. The papers themselves are published

reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2026). Potentially preventable hospitalisations in Australia by small geographic areas: 2017-18 to 2023-24. Web report, catalogue number HPF 76
task: National monitoring of hospital admissions that could have been avoided through timely care in the community - the standard system-level indicator, and the natural benchmark for judging whether prevention is shifting hospital demand
metrics: Potentially preventable hospitalisation rate per 100,000 people, adjusted for age; split into acute, chronic and vaccine-preventable groups
geoLevel: Statistical Area Level 3 (346 small areas of about 30,000-130,000 people); also Primary Health Network (33 of them), remoteness (4 categories) and socioeconomic quintile (5 groups from most to least disadvantaged)
inputData: Records of admitted hospital patients across seven financial years, 2017-18 to 2023-24
output: Counts and rates for 22 preventable conditions. In 2023-24, 778,133 hospitalisations were potentially preventable - 6.2% of all 12.6 million hospitalisations - using 3.07 million bed days, average stay 3.9 days
dataSources: National Hospital Morbidity Database; population estimates from the Australian Bureau of Statistics
accessNote: Yes - Excel and CSV are free to download. Patient-level hospital records remain restricted
scale: 868,000 rows covering 7 financial years (2017-18 to 2023-24). Covers 346 small areas, 33 Primary Health Networks, 4 remoteness categories, and 5 disadvantage quintiles.
keyAttributes: Splits by year, area, sex, age (under 65 and 65 plus), condition (22 of them) and category (acute, chronic, vaccine-preventable). Measures: number of admissions, rate per 100,000, bed days, and average length of stay

reference: Falster MO, Jorm LR, Douglas KA, Blyth FM, Elliott RF, Leyland AH (2015). Sociodemographic and health characteristics, rather than primary care supply, are major drivers of geographic variation in preventable hospitalizations in Australia. Medical Care 53(5):436-445
task: An important caution for this topic: it works out WHY preventable hospitalisation rates differ between areas, and finds the answer is mostly who lives there, not how many services are available. Guards against over-crediting or over-blaming local programs
metrics: Share of the between-area difference explained: general practitioner supply 2.9%, versus people's own social and health characteristics 36.9%
geoLevel: Statistical Local Area (199 areas across New South Wales)
inputData: 267,091 people surveyed in the 45 and Up Study (262,755 analysed after exclusions), linked to New South Wales hospital and death records; plus general practitioner supply across 199 small areas
output: General practitioner supply was NOT a significant predictor of preventable hospitalisation
dataSources: 45 and Up Study survey; New South Wales Admitted Patient Data Collection; death records; general practitioner workforce data
accessNote: No - survey and hospital records need application
keyAttributes: Per person: age, sex, income, education, smoking, physical activity, body mass index, long-term conditions. Per area: number of general practitioners. Outcome: preventable admissions

reference: Jorm LR, Leyland AH, Blyth FM, Elliott RF, Douglas KMA, Redman S, on behalf of the APHID Investigators (2012). Assessing Preventable Hospitalisation InDicators (APHID): protocol for a data-linkage study using cohort study and administrative data. BMJ Open 2:e002344
task: Sets out how to test what actually drives preventable hospitalisation at the level of individual people - the evidence chain this topic needs
metrics: Planned comparisons of preventable hospitalisation rates by health behaviour and social background
geoLevel: Individual people, New South Wales
inputData: The 45 and Up Study group of participants, linked to hospital, death and Medicare records
output: Study design and analysis plan for checking the preventable hospitalisation indicator against individual characteristics
dataSources: 45 and Up Study survey; New South Wales Admitted Patient Data Collection; Medicare and pharmaceutical records; death registry, joined together by the Centre for Health Record Linkage

reference: Vos T, Carter R, Barendregt J, Mihalopoulos C, Veerman L, Magnus A, Cobiac L, Bertram M, Wallace A (2010). Assessing Cost-Effectiveness in Prevention (ACE-Prevention): Final Report. University of Queensland & Deakin University
task: Ranks preventive interventions by value for money - the landmark Australian exercise in deciding which prevention to fund first, led by the University of Queensland
metrics: Cost per healthy year of life gained (measured as disability-adjusted life years averted); savings elsewhere in the health system
geoLevel: National
inputData: Disease data, effect sizes and costs for 123 preventive and 27 treatment interventions
output: A ranked table of interventions showing which prevention gives the best value; tax and regulatory measures came out strongest
dataSources: Australian burden of disease data; national health and population statistics; published trial evidence
accessNote: Not a dataset - the underlying models were not released

reference: World Health Organization (2018). Saving lives, spending less: a strategic response to noncommunicable diseases. Geneva: World Health Organization
task: The investment case for preventing chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes - the large-scale version of this topic's question
metrics: Return on investment per intervention; deaths avoided; healthy years of life gained
geoLevel: National (modelled across many countries)
inputData: Disease and cost data by country for the World Health Organization's recommended 'best buy' interventions
output: Projected returns: every US$1 invested returns US$7 by 2030 in lower-income countries
dataSources: World Health Organization global health estimates; country-level costing

reference: Owen L, Morgan A, Fischer A, Ellis S, Hoy A, Kelly MP (2012). The cost-effectiveness of public health interventions. Journal of Public Health 34(1):37-45
task: Shows that most public health interventions assessed for England's national clinical guidance are highly cost-effective - a counter to the claim that prevention does not pay off
metrics: Cost per quality-adjusted life year (a year of life weighted by health status)
geoLevel: National (England)
inputData: 21 economic analyses that underpinned national public health guidance issued between 2006 and 2010
output: Most results fell well within what the health system treats as good value; many interventions saved money outright
dataSources: Economic models built on English cost and disease data
accessNote: No single dataset. 200 estimates are available in the paper itself

reference: Purdy S (2010). Avoiding hospital admissions: what does the research evidence say? London: The King's Fund
task: Reviews which interventions genuinely reduce unplanned hospital admissions - a useful reality-check on the claims made about this topic
metrics: Emergency and unplanned admission rates; admissions for conditions treatable outside hospital
geoLevel: National and local (England)
inputData: Published evaluations of programs intended to avoid hospital admissions
output: Grades the evidence: some approaches work, while several widely used ones have weak or no supporting evidence
dataSources: English hospital activity statistics used in the underlying studies

reference: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (2023). Health at a Glance 2023: OECD Indicators. Paris: OECD Publishing
task: International benchmarking of avoidable admissions - places Australia alongside comparable health systems
metrics: Admissions per 100,000 people, adjusted for age and sex
geoLevel: National
inputData: National hospital discharge data submitted by member countries
output: Country-by-country comparison of avoidable admission rates for asthma, chronic lung disease, heart failure and diabetes
dataSources: OECD health statistics database
accessNote: Yes - free from the OECD portal

reference: Harriss LR, Thompson F, Lawson K, O'Loughlin M, McDermott R (2019). Preventable hospitalisations in regional Queensland: potential for primary health? Australian Health Review 43(4):371-381
task: A Queensland-specific analysis - the most locally relevant evidence in this table for where prevention could reduce hospital demand
metrics: Preventable hospitalisation rates by condition and region
geoLevel: Regional Queensland
inputData: Queensland hospital admission records for regional areas
output: Patterns of preventable hospitalisation across regional Queensland, and the share that community-based care could address
dataSources: Queensland Health admitted patient data
accessNote: No - needs application to Queensland Health
scale: Demographic data and clinical information on all admitted patients separated from both public and licensed private hospitals and private day surgeries in Queensland

reference: Joint Regional Needs Assessments, Queensland (series). Produced jointly by each Primary Health Network and its Hospital and Health Service, 2025-2027 cycle
task: Each Queensland region publishes an assessment of what its population needs and where services fall short, agreed jointly by the local Primary Health Network and hospital service. These are not datasets, but they name the priority indicators each region has settled on and say where the numbers came from - and unlike a research paper they are redone on a cycle, so they stay current. Seven Primary Health Networks means roughly seven documents. This row covers the series; Brisbane South and North Brisbane and Moreton Bay are the two linked.
metrics: Whatever each region has prioritised - typically chronic disease, obesity, smoking, mental health, alcohol and other drugs, and potentially preventable hospitalisations
geoLevel: Primary Health Network catchment and Hospital and Health Service, broken down to Statistical Area Level 2 and 3 and local government area
inputData: Population and hospital data for the region, plus consultation with local services and community
output: A free report per region setting out priority health needs and service gaps
dataSources: Brisbane South cites the Queensland Preventive Health Survey, the 2021 Census through the Queensland Government Statistician's Office, Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data, Medicare claims, and Queensland Health's non-admitted patient collection
accessNote: Free PDFs, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia. Useful mainly as a map to other people's data: they say which indicator a region cares about and which collection it came from, which is faster than working that out from scratch.
scale: One report per Primary Health Network catchment; Brisbane South covers 23 per cent of Queensland's population
keyAttributes: Priority health needs per region, with the source of each figure named

reference: Department of Health (2025). Health Indicators 2025: Snapshot series I. Population profiles. Metro South Health, Brisbane
task: A worked example of one Queensland hospital service profiling its own population down to suburb groupings, and reporting it by council area. It shows the level of detail a Queensland health service can already produce for a council-sized area, which is the question Application 6 keeps running into.
metrics: Population and projections, growth, median age, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander share, country of birth, language, and the health indicators in the wider snapshot series
geoLevel: Hospital and Health Service, local government area (Logan, Redland and southern Brisbane), and Statistical Area Level 2 and 3
inputData: Population estimates and projections, the 2021 Census, and Queensland Health collections
output: A free 64-page report with tables per area, including an appendix of the underlying figures
dataSources: Australian Bureau of Statistics population estimates and the 2021 Census; Queensland Health collections
accessNote: Free PDF, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia. The report is public; the tables come as a PDF appendix rather than a data file, so anything computed from it has to be retyped. Note the report also points at an internal Queensland Health address for an electronic version, which is not reachable from outside.
scale: 1.31 million residents, 23 per cent of Queensland, across 20 Statistical Area Level 3s and 116 Statistical Area Level 2s
keyAttributes: Population and demographic profile per area, with Queensland figures alongside for comparison

reference: World Health Organization (2013). Handbook on health inequality monitoring: with a special focus on low- and middle-income countries. Geneva: World Health Organization
task: The standard method text for this topic's core task: how to monitor health inequalities step by step
metrics: Simple difference and ratio between groups; slope index of inequality and relative index of inequality (which measure the gradient across all groups, not just the extremes); concentration index
geoLevel: Any level - the method applies anywhere
inputData: Health data broken down by wealth, education, sex, region and other population characteristics
output: A monitoring framework: choose indicators, choose the population splits, calculate summary measures, report the results
dataSources: Household surveys and routine administrative records
accessNote: Not a dataset

reference: Marmot M, Allen J, Boyce T, Goldblatt P, Morrison J (2020). Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On. London: Institute of Health Equity / The Health Foundation
task: The source of 'proportionate universalism' - the targeting logic this topic asks about, meaning prevention is offered to everyone but with effort scaled up in more disadvantaged places. Also tracks a decade of inequality trends
metrics: Gaps in life expectancy and healthy life expectancy between the most and least deprived tenths of the population
geoLevel: National down to neighbourhood
inputData: Life expectancy, death rates and social indicators from 2010 to 2020
output: Finds inequalities widened and life expectancy stopped improving; sets out recommendations across six policy areas
dataSources: National death and population statistics; the English Index of Multiple Deprivation (a small-area measure of disadvantage)
accessNote: Yes
keyAttributes: Deprivation files: rank and decile per neighbourhood

reference: Flavel J, Kedzior SGE, Isaac V, Cameron D, Baum F (2024). Regional health inequalities in Australia and social determinants of health: analysis of trends and distribution by remoteness. Rural and Remote Health 24:7726
task: The closest match in this table to this topic's core question, and it covers rural and remote Australia explicitly. The key point: differences WITHIN non-city areas are large, so regions and towns should not be lumped together when targeting prevention
metrics: Slope index of inequality across disadvantage groups - a measure of the whole gradient, which the authors argue is better than simply comparing the most and least disadvantaged groups
geoLevel: Local government area (538 of them), grouped by how remote they are, and capital city versus rest of state
inputData: Public Health Information Development Unit data for capital cities, the rest of each state and territory, and 538 local government areas; trends from 1986 to 2018
output: Premature and avoidable death rates fell everywhere, but the gap between richer and poorer areas WIDENED outside the capital cities; social conditions showed mixed trends
dataSources: Public Health Information Development Unit small-area data (Torrens University); Australian Bureau of Statistics disadvantage rankings; death and census records

reference: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care and Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2021). The Fourth Australian Atlas of Healthcare Variation. Sydney: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care. ISBN 978-1-922563-06-4
task: Maps healthcare use and preventable hospitalisation by small area, split by disadvantage, remoteness and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status. Chapter 2 covers preventable hospitalisations. Notes a key gap: Indigenous status is missing from Medicare and pharmaceutical data, and undercounted in hospital data
metrics: Rates per 100,000 people adjusted for age and sex; 'magnitude of variation', meaning the highest area rate divided by the lowest. Chronic lung disease varies 18.1-fold between areas, and is 4.8 times higher for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
geoLevel: Statistical Area Level 3 (about 30,000-130,000 people); also grouped by Primary Health Network, state, remoteness and disadvantage
inputData: Hospital records 2014-15 to 2017-18; Medicare and pharmaceutical records 2018-19; birth records 2017; population estimates as denominators
output: Maps and tables of standardised rates by small area for 18 clinical items, each with equity breakdowns. Chapter 2 covers 330,000+ preventable hospitalisations in 2017-18 across five conditions
dataSources: National Hospital Morbidity Database; Medicare Benefits Schedule; Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme; National Perinatal Data Collection; population, remoteness and disadvantage classifications
accessNote: No - underlying records are not released

reference: Canadian Institute for Health Information (2018). In Pursuit of Health Equity: Defining Stratifiers for Measuring Health Inequality - A Focus on Age, Sex, Gender, Income, Education and Geographic Location. Ottawa: Canadian Institute for Health Information
task: Answers this topic's 'what data is missing' question: it standardises WHICH population characteristics should be recorded alongside health data so that fair comparisons are possible
metrics: Definitions of each population split, and the equity gap measured for each
geoLevel: National and provincial
inputData: A review of existing Canadian health databases, checking which population characteristics they capture
output: Recommended standard definitions for six population characteristics, plus guidance on building them into data collection
dataSources: Canadian administrative health data linked to census records
accessNote: No for the health records

reference: Flanagan BE, Gregory EW, Hallisey EJ, Heitgerd JL, Lewis B (2011). A Social Vulnerability Index for Disaster Management. Journal of Homeland Security and Emergency Management 8(1), Article 3
sourceType: Peer-reviewed, plus a government data tool
task: A widely reused composite index for identifying vulnerable areas - a working model for how Queensland could build its own index to target prevention
metrics: A percentile ranking per theme plus an overall ranking (so an area can be placed against all others)
geoLevel: Census tract (roughly neighbourhood size)
inputData: United States census and community survey variables
output: A vulnerability ranking for every small area, across four themes: social and economic position, household composition, ethnicity and language, and housing and transport
dataSources: United States Census Bureau American Community Survey
accessNote: Yes - the index files are free to download, no registration

reference: Atkinson J, Salmond C, Crampton P, Viggers H, Lacey K (2024). NZDep2023 Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation: Research Report. Wellington: University of Otago
task: A small-area disadvantage index used routinely in New Zealand to allocate health funding and target services - a proven mechanism for turning disadvantage data into prevention resourcing
metrics: The nine variables combined into a single score, then sorted into ten equal groups from 1 (least disadvantaged) to 10 (most disadvantaged)
geoLevel: Small area (roughly a few hundred people), which can be added up to any larger level
inputData: Nine variables from the 2023 census covering eight aspects of disadvantage: income, employment, communication, support, qualifications, home ownership, living space and dry housing
output: A disadvantage score and rank for every small area in New Zealand
dataSources: New Zealand Census of Population and Dwellings 2023
accessNote: Yes for the finished index
scale: ~32,000 small areas covering all of New Zealand, generally 100-200 residents each
keyAttributes: Nine census variables (income, employment, communication, support, qualifications, home ownership, space, damp housing), combined into one score reported as deciles 1-10

reference: Maiam nayri Wingara Indigenous Data Sovereignty Collective and Australian Indigenous Governance Institute (2018). Indigenous Data Sovereignty Communique, Indigenous Data Sovereignty Summit, 20 June 2018, Canberra
task: Speaks to how inequity can be reported responsibly: it asserts Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' rights over how data about them is created, accessed and interpreted, countering the negative framing that can itself entrench disadvantage
metrics: Not applicable - these are criteria to apply when choosing and reporting equity indicators
geoLevel: All levels
inputData: Not applicable - these are governance principles that apply to any Indigenous data
output: A statement of Indigenous data sovereignty rights and data governance principles
dataSources: Applies to all datasets about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

reference: Public Health Information Development Unit (PHIDU). Social Health Atlas of Australia. Adelaide: Torrens University Australia
task: Brings health, social and economic figures for small areas together in one place so differences between areas can be seen side by side. It is the usual starting point in Australia for asking which areas are worse off and on what.
metrics: Chronic disease, health risk factors, socioeconomic position, and use of health services, with separate sets for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations, older people, and children and young people
geoLevel: Local government area, Primary Health Network, Statistical Area Level 3, and Population Health Area
inputData: Census, administrative health collections and national surveys, compiled per area
output: Downloadable spreadsheets and maps, one workbook per geographic structure
dataSources: Australian Bureau of Statistics collections, Medicare and other administrative health data, national surveys
accessNote: Free Excel workbooks, no registration. Attribution conditions apply - check the copyright page before republishing anything.
scale: All of Australia at small-area level
keyAttributes: One row per area, one column per indicator, with the Australian rate alongside for comparison

reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2023). Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA), Australia, 2021. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
task: Ranks every area in Australia by social and economic disadvantage, from census answers. It is what most Australian work means when it says 'the most disadvantaged areas', so using it makes results comparable with everyone else's.
metrics: Four indexes: Relative Socio-economic Disadvantage; Relative Socio-economic Advantage and Disadvantage; Economic Resources; and Education and Occupation. Each is reported as a score, a rank, a decile and a quintile.
geoLevel: Statistical Area Level 1 and 2, local government area, and larger areas
inputData: Census variables covering income, education, employment, occupation, housing and other household characteristics
output: A score and a rank for every area, with areas also sorted into tenths and fifths
dataSources: Census of Population and Housing 2021
accessNote: Free Excel downloads, no registration.
scale: Every area in Australia, rebuilt after each census
keyAttributes: Index score, national and state rank, decile and quintile per area

reference: Higgs C, Badland H, Simons K, Knibbs LD, Giles-Corti B (2019). The Urban Liveability Index: developing a policy-relevant urban liveability composite measure and evaluating associations with transport mode choice. International Journal of Health Geographics 18:14
task: How to build and test a liveability index that is detailed enough to guide policy - the method this topic would follow
metrics: The overall liveability score and each of its component measures
geoLevel: Individual street addresses, which can be added up to larger areas
inputData: Liveability measures calculated for every residential address in Melbourne: walkability, transport, open space, employment, housing affordability and community facilities
output: A combined liveability score for each address, checked against how people actually travel
dataSources: Census and disadvantage data; a Victorian travel survey; mapped infrastructure data
accessNote: Yes
scale: The survey is conducted throughout the year across greater Melbourne, and periodically in Geelong and other key regional centres. Over 32,000 households contributed to this survey since 2012
keyAttributes: Travel survey comes as six linked files: households, persons, trips, stops, journey to work, journey to education

reference: Higgs C, Lowe M, Hooper P, Mavoa S, Arundel J, Gunn L, Simons K, Giles-Corti B (2023). Policy relevant health related liveability indicator datasets for addresses in Australia's 21 largest cities. Scientific Data 10:113
task: Publishes the underlying liveability datasets as free open data - so an agency could calculate these indicators itself rather than paying for dashboard access
metrics: Neighbourhood liveability and access-to-amenity measures
geoLevel: Street address, which can be added up to larger areas
inputData: Built environment measures for addresses across Australia's 21 largest cities
output: Free downloadable datasets of liveability indicators, at address level and for administrative areas
dataSources: Census data, OpenStreetMap (a free public map), public transport timetable data and government mapping data
accessNote: Yes - published as open data by RMIT University. The repository blocks automated checks, so open the link in a browser
scale: Residential address points across Australia's 21 largest cities

reference: Giles-Corti B, Vernez-Moudon A, Reis R, Turrell G, Dannenberg AL, Badland H, Foster S, Lowe M, Sallis JF, Stevenson M, Owen N (2016). City planning and population health: a global challenge. The Lancet 388:2912-2924
task: Identifies eight city-planning levers that together encourage walking, cycling and public transport - the reasoning that links this topic's indicator areas to actual health outcomes
metrics: The eight planning levers, and their links to chronic disease and road trauma
geoLevel: City and neighbourhood
inputData: A global review of evidence on city form, transport and health
output: A framework plus supporting evidence for the eight planning levers
dataSources: Published studies from many countries

reference: Boeing G, Higgs C, Liu S, Giles-Corti B, Sallis JF, Cerin E, et al. (2022). Using open data and open-source software to develop spatial indicators of urban design and transport features for achieving healthy and sustainable cities. Lancet Global Health 10(6):e907-e918
task: A reusable, freely available process for calculating comparable indicators within and between cities - the template for a framework that could scale across Queensland
metrics: Walkability; access to fresh food, public transport and open space; whether planning policy targets are being met
geoLevel: Small grids and neighbourhoods within each city
inputData: Free public map data, public transport timetable data, and official population maps
output: Indicators for 25 cities, allowing comparison both within a city and between cities
dataSources: Entirely free and public data sources, processed with freely available software
accessNote: The toolkit is open source
keyAttributes: Population and street density, street connectivity, walkability, and distance to fresh food, shops, public transport and open space

reference: Lowe M, Whitzman C, Badland H, Davern M, Aye L, Hes D, Butterworth I, Giles-Corti B (2015). Planning Healthy, Liveable and Sustainable Cities: How Can Indicators Inform Policy? Urban Policy and Research 33(2):131-144
task: Directly answers this topic's design question: what makes indicators actually get picked up and used by decision-makers
metrics: Criteria for choosing and using indicators
geoLevel: City and local government area
inputData: A review of Australian and international liveability indicator systems, plus interviews with academics and decision-makers
output: Recommendations for making indicators policy-relevant: match them to the levers government actually controls, report them at a useful geographic detail, and communicate them well
dataSources: Existing indicator systems; stakeholder interview data

reference: Gourevitch MN, Athens JK, Levine SE, Kleiman N, Thorpe LE (2019). City-Level Measures of Health, Health Determinants, and Equity to Foster Population Health Improvement: The City Health Dashboard. American Journal of Public Health 109(4):585-592
sourceType: Peer-reviewed, plus a live public dashboard
task: A mature working example of what this topic is aiming at: standardised local health measures delivered to city governments to prompt action
metrics: Measures covering health outcomes, social and economic conditions, health behaviours, physical environment and clinical care
geoLevel: City and census tract (roughly neighbourhood size)
inputData: National health surveys, birth and death records, and federal administrative data
output: A web dashboard of 37 measures across five areas for the 500 largest United States cities, at both city and neighbourhood level (the live version has since grown)
dataSources: Census and community survey data; national disease control data; environmental agency data; birth and death records

reference: Topp CW, Ostergaard SD, Sondergaard S, Bech P (2015). The WHO-5 Well-Being Index: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics 84(3):167-176
task: Evidence on whether the five-question WHO-5 wellbeing measure actually works. This is exactly the 'is this measure valid and reliable' test this topic calls for, and the measure is already in use on Queensland indicator lists
metrics: The WHO-5 score (five questions); how well it detects what it is meant to detect; how responsive it is to change
geoLevel: Individual people, which can be added up to any area
inputData: Studies that used the five-question WHO-5 wellbeing questionnaire, in both clinical and general population settings
output: Finds the measure performs well both for screening and for tracking change over time, and works across many different settings
dataSources: Survey data collected in the reviewed studies
accessNote: No primary dataset; questionnaire free to use

reference: Lytle LA, Sokol RL (2017). Measures of the food environment: A systematic review of the field, 2007-2015. Health & Place 44:18-34
task: Assesses whether measures of the local food environment are actually reliable - directly relevant to healthy eating indicators such as outlet density, supermarket access and the cost of a healthy food basket
metrics: Counts of food outlets and how close they are; in-store audits; the costed healthy food basket; survey questions about how people perceive their local food options
geoLevel: Neighbourhood and small area
inputData: Studies published between 2007 and 2015 that measured food environments
output: A critique of measurement quality across the field, finding that many measures have never been properly tested for reliability or accuracy
dataSources: Business listings mapped geographically, in-store audit tools, and survey measures
accessNote: Not a dataset

reference: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development & European Commission Joint Research Centre (2008). Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators: Methodology and User Guide. Paris: OECD Publishing
task: The standard method text for this topic's goal of a combined index or dashboard: how to weight and combine indicators, and how to test whether the result holds up
metrics: Ways to put indicators on a common scale and weight them; techniques for checking how sensitive the final ranking is to those choices
geoLevel: Any
inputData: Any set of candidate indicators intended to be combined into a single score
output: A ten-step framework, from setting out the underlying concept through to presenting and publishing the results
dataSources: Applies to whatever indicator set the user supplies

reference: Queensland Health. Preventive health survey series and the Queensland survey analytic system (QSAS). Brisbane: Queensland Health (ongoing series)
task: Queensland's own repeated telephone survey of adults and children, reporting how many people meet health guidelines and how that differs between parts of the state. This is the closest thing in the scan to a ready-made Queensland answer for a council-sized area, and the only source here that reports at local government area, Hospital and Health Service and Primary Health Network at once.
metrics: Adults: overweight and obesity, daily smoking, physical activity, fruit and vegetable intake, alcohol, sunburn and sun protection. Children: the equivalent child indicators.
geoLevel: Queensland, Hospital and Health Service, Primary Health Network and local government area for adults; Queensland, Hospital and Health Service and Primary Health Network for children
inputData: Telephone interviews with a random sample of Queensland residents. Regional figures pool two survey years together so the numbers are large enough to report.
output: Percentages by region and by sociodemographic group, through an interactive viewer, plus spreadsheets on the Queensland open data portal.
dataSources: Queensland preventive health telephone survey
accessNote: Free, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Note the years do not agree between sources: the open data portal record lists adult surveys 2009-10 to 2015-16, while the Brisbane South needs assessment cites QPHS 2017-2022, so later years exist somewhere. Worth asking the agency which years they can actually get.
scale: A statewide random sample, pooled over two years for regional reporting
keyAttributes: Region, age, sex and sociodemographic group, against each health indicator

reference: Queensland Government Statistician's Office. Queensland regional profiles and the Queensland regional database. Brisbane: Queensland Treasury
task: Builds a statistical profile of any Queensland region on request, including a region the user defines by combining smaller areas. It is the general-purpose background picture of a council area - who lives there, how they are employed, how the population is changing - rather than a health source.
metrics: Population and projections, age and sex, country of birth, education, disability, long-term health conditions, employment and income, business counts, building approvals, recorded offences
geoLevel: Local government area, Statistical Area Level 2 to 4, Greater Capital City Statistical Area, state electoral district, or a custom region built from Statistical Area Level 2 pieces
inputData: Census, population estimates and projections, and administrative collections held across Queensland Government
output: A profile report as PDF or web page. The companion regional database gives the same kind of figures as a time series that can be pulled out directly.
dataSources: Australian Bureau of Statistics collections and Queensland Government administrative data
accessNote: Free and no registration. The profile tool gives finished reports rather than a data file, so it answers a question rather than feeding a calculation - use the regional database for figures you need to work with.
scale: All of Queensland, down to suburb-sized areas
keyAttributes: Demographic, social and economic characteristics per region

reference: Australian Urban Observatory. Liveability indicators for Australian cities. Melbourne: RMIT University Centre for Urban Research
task: Maps liveability across Australia's larger cities and reports it back to councils and planners. It is the finished, maintained version of the liveability work already in this table as sources 1 and 2 of this application.
metrics: Walkability, public transport access, access to supermarkets and grocers, public open space, social infrastructure, employment, housing, alcohol outlet access, and area demographics
geoLevel: Local government area, suburb and neighbourhood, across 21 Australian cities including Brisbane
inputData: The national liveability indicator datasets built from census, mapping and public transport data
output: Interactive maps and area scores for each liveability domain
dataSources: The Australian national liveability datasets produced by the same team
accessNote: Seeing the mapped data needs a paid partnership - the site's own wording is 'Become a Paid Partner to see Liveability Mapped'. Worth knowing before anyone plans around it. The underlying 2018 national liveability dataset is free and open, and is already in this table as source 2 of this application (Higgs et al. 2023), so the measures can be obtained without the subscription if someone is willing to do the processing.
keyAttributes: A score per liveability domain for each small area

reference: Global Observatory of Healthy and Sustainable Cities. 1000 Cities Challenge. Melbourne: RMIT University
task: Computes the same set of city measures the same way in every participating city, so one city can be compared against another rather than only against itself. Brisbane is one of the cities included. The method behind it is source 4 of this application.
metrics: Population within walking distance of public transport, fresh food and public open space; street connectivity; walkability; population density. Alongside these, policy measures covering transport, air quality, parking, cycling and walking infrastructure, and housing density rules.
geoLevel: Whole city, and smaller areas within a city
inputData: Open mapping and transport data for each city, plus a policy questionnaire completed locally
output: A scorecard and report per city, and the spatial indicators behind them
dataSources: OpenStreetMap and equivalent open data, plus locally completed policy scorecards
accessNote: The scorecards and reports are published free. What is downloadable, and on what terms, is not stated on the site - it would need an email to the team. The software and method are open, through source 4 of this application.
scale: Around 80 cities across six continents, including Adelaide, Brisbane, Canberra, Melbourne and Sydney
keyAttributes: Spatial and policy indicators per city

reference: Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Liveable Communities. Urban Liveability Checklist. Melbourne: RMIT University Centre for Urban Research
task: A checklist a planner works through to judge whether a place, built or proposed, supports health and wellbeing. It turns the liveability research into something someone can apply to a development without needing the data first.
metrics: The built-environment features shown to support health and wellbeing, as a checklist rather than as scored measures
geoLevel: A single neighbourhood or development site
inputData: Local knowledge of the area being assessed
output: A completed assessment of an area against the built-environment features the research links to health
dataSources: Not applicable - it is applied to a place, not computed from a dataset
accessNote: Free PDF from the page above. It produces an assessment rather than data, so nothing is downloadable from it.
scale: One site or neighbourhood at a time

reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2022). Census of Population and Housing, 2021. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
task: Counts everyone in the country every five years. It matters here because it is the only source that measures how people travel to work, and how many people volunteer, for every small area in Queensland at once - two of the measures on the agency's own list that nothing else in this table covers.
metrics: Method of travel to work, which gives active transport mode share directly; voluntary work for an organisation; unpaid domestic work and unpaid care; long-term health conditions; plus the usual population, income, housing and employment counts
geoLevel: Released down to Statistical Area Level 1, and for local government areas, suburbs and larger areas
inputData: A form completed by every household on census night
output: Counts and cross-tabulations for any area, as downloadable packs or built to order in the online table tool
dataSources: The census itself
accessNote: Free, no registration. Downloadable area packs, or build a table to order online.
scale: Every household in Australia, every five years; 2021 is the latest
keyAttributes: Method of travel to work (MTWP), voluntary work (VOLWP), unpaid domestic work (DOMP), unpaid care (UNCAREP), long-term health conditions (LTHP)
